name: Ara-290

lead: ARA 290 (cibinetide) is a short peptide derived from erythropoietin, designed to trigger tissue-protective signalling without boosting red blood cells. Recovery-focused users discuss it for tissue protection and nerve healing.

It is designed to activate the innate repair receptor, which researchers describe as mediating tissue protection and anti-inflammation, while avoiding the hematologic effects of EPO. Small exploratory trials in sarcoidosis and type 2 diabetes neuropathy reported symptom and nerve-fibre improvements.

paras: It is investigational and has no approved use. In peptide communities it is discussed as a repair-oriented compound for recovery, though human data come from small patient trials rather than healthy trainees.
Safety data come from small patient trials. It is investigational with no approved use, and its effects in healthy people have not been studied.

angle.text: ARA 290 is an EPO-derived peptide that activates a tissue repair receptor, and recovery-focused users discuss it for faster tissue healing and better recovery between sessions. It has been tested in small neuropathy trials in sarcoidosis and diabetes.

lead: ARA 290, also known as cibinetide, is an 11-amino-acid peptide engineered from the structure of erythropoietin (EPO). It was designed to activate the innate repair receptor involved in tissue protection without raising red blood cell counts, avoiding the thrombosis risk associated with recombinant EPO.[1][2][3] Within peptide-focused communities it is grouped with 'regenerative' peptides such as BPC-157, TB-500 and GHK-Cu, and the appearance case that proponents make is recovery and tissue repair: faster healing, calmer inflammation and nerve protection that could mean more consistent training and better-healed skin and tissue.[4]

It was developed by Araim Pharmaceuticals and has been tested in small human trials of neuropathic symptoms in sarcoidosis and type 2 diabetes.[3][5][6][7] Authors of these studies reported symptom and nerve-fibre improvements, but the trials were small and exploratory.[5][6][7] No human study of ARA 290 for appearance, recovery or performance has been published; the closest work on skin is a mouse study of wound healing in genetic diabetes.[8]
infobox: Cibinetide, ARA290, pHBSP, pyroglutamate helix B surface peptide [3]

paras: ARA 290 is a short peptide of 11 amino acids (sequence UEQLERALNSS, with an N-terminal pyroglutamate) and a molar mass of about 1,257 g/mol. Its alternative name, pyroglutamate helix B surface peptide, points to a segment of erythropoietin's helix B, the part associated with tissue protection rather than red cell production.[3][1] Modified versions with longer duration of action have been described.[3]

Erythropoietin is best known as the hormone that stimulates red blood cell production. Researchers observed that it also protects tissue under stress, and that this effect is mediated through a different receptor arrangement (the EPO receptor paired with the beta common receptor, sometimes called the innate repair receptor) from the one that drives red blood cell production.[1][8]

ARA 290 is discussed in the same breath as other regenerative peptides in the context of tissue repair and chronic pain management, but a 2026 review of regenerative peptides states that the evidence behind such compounds differs by peptide and is mostly preclinical outside a few agents.[4] A 2026 narrative review of regenerative peptides for jaw nerve injury lists ARA-290 among candidates whose reported functions overlap with nerve regeneration mechanisms, noting that direct evidence in that injury remains inadequate.[9]

For looks, the relevant research is a mouse study reporting that activation of the EPO receptor and beta common receptor complex by cibinetide improved impaired wound healing in diabetic mice.[8] Community discussion specific to this peptide is sparse, and no user reports of its effect on appearance have been published in the research literature.

Clinical development has centred on neuropathic pain and small fibre neuropathy in sarcoidosis and type 2 diabetes, where the peptide was tested for symptom scores and corneal nerve fibre measurements.[3][5][6][7] A systematic review of fatigue treatments in sarcoidosis identified ARA 290 among six interventions studied.[10] A review of diabetic neuropathy drug development mentions cibinetide among agents under study, noting that approved agents relieve pain without affecting the underlying pathology.[11]

Researchers describe a tissue-protection system mediated by locally produced hyposialated EPO that activates an innate repair receptor, triggered by cellular stress. Recombinant EPO is limited for this purpose by rises in hematocrit and platelet activation; ARA 290 was engineered to activate the repair receptor without these effects.[1][2] Preclinical studies reported long-term relief of neuropathic pain with suppression of the spinal microglia response, and protection of transplanted islets in animal models through inhibition of macrophage activation.[12][13]

Other animal studies reported effects in experimental autoimmune neuritis, experimental colitis, and in ageing mouse hearts, where cibinetide reduced cardiac inflammation and was associated with longer healthspan.[14][15][16]

Araim Pharmaceuticals developed the peptide from the helix B region of erythropoietin.[3][1] The first randomised pilot study in sarcoidosis was published in 2012, followed by a corneal nerve fibre report in 2013, a diabetes study in 2015 and a phase 2b trial of 64 patients in 2017.[5][6][7][17] Development for depressive disorders was discontinued, according to Wikipedia.[3]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study enrolled 22 sarcoidosis patients with symptoms of small fibre neuropathy, giving ARA 290 three times weekly, and was published in 2012.[5] A 2013 report described improved symptoms and increased corneal nerve fibre density in sarcoidosis patients with small nerve fibre loss.[6] A 2014 review of two phase 2 trials said treatment was consistently associated with improvement in neuropathic pain scores, increases in corneal nerve fibres, improved sensory pain thresholds, quality of life and physical functioning.[2]

A phase 2b, 28-day randomized trial of 64 subjects with sarcoid-associated small nerve fibre loss and neuropathic pain assessed corneal nerve fibre area and regenerating fibres as surrogate endpoints [17]; the trial was registered in 2014 [18].

A 2015 study in patients with type 2 diabetes and painful neuropathy reported improved metabolic control and neuropathic symptoms.[7] A registered Phase 2 trial in prediabetes and type 2 diabetes enrolled 24 participants,[19] and a Phase 2 trial in diabetic macular oedema was terminated after about 9 participants.[20] A review summarised the clinical development in sarcoidosis neuropathy.[2]
No studies were found of ARA 290 in healthy people or for cosmetic, recovery or performance outcomes.

The published pilot studies describe the peptide as tested for safety alongside efficacy, in small groups. Long-term and large-scale safety data are not available.[5][7] The design aim was to avoid the red cell and clotting effects of recombinant EPO.[1] Because it is an investigational injectable peptide, the quality of products outside trials is not overseen the way approved drugs are.
